What you are missing is scale and precision.

Every map projection has different levels of inaccuracy, but are good for "small enough" areas. This is why each state uses its own map projection (some states are large enough that they need two) and coordinate system and if you do surveying across state lines it is a pain in the ass to convert between the two. If you are doing work that requires less accuracy (you don't care if you are off by inches), geoid models are good enough to where differences in actual geography don't make all that much of a difference. The truth is that the earth is so large that the curvature in a given area is so gradual that treating it as flat or using an approximation of the curvature only causes inaccuracies of a very small amount. This is why on maps some countries look gigantic, but the ones in the middle are generally pretty accurate. The farther away from the center of the projection that you use, the more inaccurate it will be, so if you set up the grid to a small enough area everything works.
